item.title: Residential escape: Urbanization and emerging middle-class politics in the Global South
item.description:
Jeffrey W. Paller
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261506219
There is an ongoing debate about whether urbanization in the Global South will strengthen democracy or undermine it by deepening socio-economic inequalities. These theories are based on an underlying assumption that the emerging middle class holds democratic attitudes and engages in democratic practices. In this debates paper , I introduce the concept of residential escape to better reflect the emerging middle-class politics extending across Global South cities today. Residential escape refers to the urban secession of middle- and upper-classes from the city through the creation of spatial and class boundaries and the establishment of local control in new territories and neighborhoods. The results have contradictory consequences for democratization. On the one hand, residential escape opens up new avenues for citizen participation, spaces of representation, and opportunities for urban claim-making. On the other hand, it separates poor, middle-, and upper-class populations through residential segregation, eroding the potential of the urban commons. Drawing on examples from Asia, Africa, and Latin America, the paper advocates an approach to middle-class politics that embraces the contradictions and ambiguities of the democratic process.

item.title: Towards a relational understanding of visibility: Queer spatial strategies and agency in Beirut
item.description:
Jean Makhlouta
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261506226
This paper develops the notion of relational visibility to rethink how access to urban space is negotiated beyond the binary opposition between visibility and invisibility. Queer visibility in Beirut offers a particularly heuristic case, as it is shaped both by constraining legal and social frameworks and by shifting forms of tolerance. Drawing on 11 months of ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2021 and 2023, the analysis examines how sexual and gender minorities manage exposure, discretion and recognition across different public spaces. It focuses on three urban sites that structure contrasting relational settings and forms of public legibility: the Corniche, security checkpoints and the squares occupied during the October 2019 uprising. The paper shows that visibility is not a fixed condition but an intersubjective and spatial process, continuously recalibrated according to the relational dynamics specific to each setting. It also foregrounds forms of agency anchored in space and the everyday that are too often overlooked in Middle Eastern contexts. More broadly, the paper argues that the right to the city depends less on a universal right to visibility than on the capacity to regulate one’s perceptibility across uneven configurations of power.

item.title: From occupied universities to architectural sanctuaries: Spatial politics of student resistance in Serbia, 2024–2025
item.description:
Biljana Arandelovic
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261506526
Serbian students occupied university buildings from November 2024 to September 2025 in one of contemporary Europe’s longest university occupations, triggered by the Novi Sad railway station collapse. Campuses functioned as urban infrastructure of resistance, enabling horizontal governance under institutional capture. Building on observation within occupied universities, this commentary introduces the architectural sanctuary as an overarching concept and develops three operational concepts: academic territorialization, plenum sovereignty, and dormitory amphitheaters. These concepts explain how students organized access, decision-making, and material culture while shifting across three modes of blockade: continuous physical inhabitation, administrative disruption without overnight presence, and calibrated sanctuary that combined selective permeability with partial institutional support. After most physical occupations were dismantled between July and September 2025, the movement persisted through administrative blockades, with the State University of Novi Pazar remaining the most durable outlier until January 2026. The state response relied less on spectacular repression than on administrative violence, using bureaucratic pressure to fracture student–faculty solidarity. Reading the occupied buildings as architecture, the commentary shows how occupation reorganized their interiors, thresholds and use, and how the state contested the occupations through the same buildings.

item.title: Institutional arrangements and growth coalition restructuring in urban village renovation: A comparative analysis of multiple governance modes in Guangzhou
item.description:
Manman Xia, Xiaodong Yang, Jiayu Zhang
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261506824
Existing studies on urban village renovation (UVR) in China have highlighted the importance of governance arrangements and state intervention, but have paid less attention to how changing institutional conditions continuously reshape coalition relations over time. Drawing on policy analysis and comparative case studies in Guangzhou, this study examines how institutional change transforms governance modes and restructures growth coalitions. Using the analytical framework of “institutional arrangement-governance mode-alliance relationship,” this study compares governance modes under different institutional conditions and reveals how institutional change restructures coalitions. The findings show that changing institutional arrangements reshape participation rules, resource allocation, implementation responsibilities, and bargaining conditions, thereby altering actor roles, power relations, and coordination mechanisms. Rather than representing a linear transition, UVR involves the reconfiguration of governance modes through interactions between institutional restructuring and implementation feedback. These changes demonstrate that growth coalitions are not fixed configurations based solely on shared development interests, but relational arrangements whose stability and coordination are continuously reconstituted through institutional change. The findings also offer broader insights into coalition restructuring in other strong-state developmental contexts.

item.title: Aspiring to be dense in Indonesia’s smart kampungs
item.description:
Orlando Woods
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261507009
This paper explores how networked density is harnessed to advance a vision of a desired urban future. Network thinking captures both the inter-city networks of policy and knowledge transfer that connect different scales of governance and the intra-city networks that constitute the digital infrastructures of the smart city. Networks have space-transcending characteristics that can cause topological understandings of density to rub up against more topographical spatial realities. I illustrate these ideas by considering the emergence of ‘smart kampungs’ in the Banyuwangi Regency of Indonesia and how density is deployed in the service of national- and regional-scale policy ambitions and agendas. Indonesia’s 100 Smart Cities movement and the ASEAN Smart Cities Network are designed to achieve a critical mass of smart cities to signal urban progress and success. Implicated within these ambitions are Banyuwangi’s smart kampungs, which are positioned at the tail-end of urban development in Indonesia and are defined by socio-spatial sprawl across primarily agricultural land. The developmental logics underpinning smart kampungs reveal the role of density in creating networked demands, infrastructural aspirations, and alternative visions of urban futurity.
